title: A 2,000-year-old Greek device used bronze gears to predict eclipses

cover.alt: The largest surviving fragment of the Antikythera mechanism: corroded green bronze with a big toothed gear wheel visible.

body: In 1901 divers pulled a lump of corroded bronze from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera. It turned out to be the **oldest known analogue computer**: a hand-cranked box of interlocking gears that showed where the Sun and Moon stood in the zodiac, the phase of the Moon, and when eclipses were due, using the 223-month Saros cycle. Scans in 2005 suggested about 35 bronze gears, the largest 13 cm across with 223 teeth. Scholars date it to somewhere between the late 3rd and early 1st century BC, and nothing of similar complexity appears again until the clocks of 14th-century Europe.

slides.alt: Several corroded bronze fragments of the Antikythera mechanism displayed in a museum case.
slides.caption: Fragments of the mechanism in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens. 82 pieces are known; seven carry the important gearing.

slides.question: How many fragments of the mechanism are known today?
slides.explanation: 82 fragments are known, but only seven are mechanically significant. The largest, Fragment A, holds the big four-spoked gear.

slides.heading: Ahead of its time
slides.text: The gears' triangular teeth have an average pitch of just 1.6 mm. Machines with similar complexity did not appear again until the 14th century in western Europe. The fragments are kept in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

slides.question: What made the Moon pointer speed up and slow down, as the real Moon does?
options: A pin riding in a slot between two gears
The user turning the crank unevenly
slides.explanation: Two gears form an epicyclic pair: a pin on one gear moves back and forth in a slot on the other, varying the output speed to model the Moon's elliptical orbit.
